(CNN) -- While the spotlight of Oscar night seemed fixed firmly on "Slumdog Millionaire," one remarkably brave young girl found herself captivated by another India-based film at the ceremony. Like millions of children in developing countries, she had once endured a facial deformity and the harsh social consequences that accompanied it. The film, "Smile Pinki," was also an Oscar contender—nominated for Best Documentary Short Subject, an award it ultimately claimed on Sunday night.

The young girl watching the ceremony unfold had traveled an extraordinary distance to be there: all the way from her small Indian village to Los Angeles, California, accompanied by her father. For Pinki Sonkar, it had been nothing short of a remarkable journey. "Smile Pinki" chronicles her transformation from a sorrowful outcast into a spirited eight-year-old brimming with confidence.

Pinki was born with a cleft lip, a condition her impoverished family lacked the means to correct. Like countless other children afflicted with this deformity in the developing world, she had no choice but to endure it—along with the social stigma that followed. Her father, Rajendra Sonkar, recalls: "She used to go to school and the kids would not befriend her. She would say, 'I don't want to go to school.'"

*Watch how Pinki was transformed by the operation »*

"Pinki was a depressed, sad, lonely, shy young girl, growing up on the periphery of society in a small village," said Satish Kalra, director of Smile Train's South Asian region, recounting his impressions after meeting her. Even her own family, Kalra notes, had felt a sense of shame because of her condition.

But everything has since changed. Today, Pinki is a spirited, energetic, and confident young girl—complete with a radiant new smile, thanks to the Smile Train charity. The organization trains local doctors to perform cleft lip surgeries, addressing a deformity that affects as many as four million children worldwide.

*iReport: Share your Oscar predictions*

The film's director, Megan Mylan, has received numerous accolades throughout her career—but never before an Oscar, until now. For Pinki and her father, witnessing the director's Oscar win would undoubtedly be thrilling. Yet they understand that they already possess the greatest reward of all: Pinki's new smile.

"I am so happy that my daughter's lips have been repaired," Rajendra said, smiling, as he expressed his hope that the film would inspire others to help children whose families cannot afford such life-changing surgery.

For Pinki's family, who lived in poverty, the idea of corrective surgery seemed like an impossible dream, both financially and logistically out of reach.

Her father, a poor rickshaw puller, wanted desperately to help his daughter but lacked the resources to pursue treatment. Pinki grew up believing that her face would forever define—and limit—her life.

## A Life-Changing Intervention

Everything changed when Pinki was connected with the Smile Train organization, a nonprofit dedicated to providing free cleft surgery to children in developing countries. Through local health workers and volunteers who identified children in need across India's villages, Pinki's story reached those who could offer the medical intervention she needed.

The corrective surgery she underwent was relatively simple by modern medical standards—a procedure that takes less than an hour in many cases—but its impact on her life was immeasurable. For the first time, Pinki could smile freely, speak clearly, and face the world without fear of ridicule.

## "Smile Pinki": A Documentary That Changed Everything

It didn't sensationalize Pinki's story—instead, it presented her simply as a child who deserved the chance to smile, to attend school without shame, and to be seen as more than her condition.

## The Academy Awards: A Dream Beyond Imagination

In 2009, "Smile Pinki" won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject. For a girl who once believed she would spend her life hidden away in her village, the news that her story had reached Hollywood was almost unfathomable.

## A Legacy of Awareness and Advocacy

Pinki's journey did more than change her own life—it brought international attention to the millions of children worldwide living with untreated cleft conditions, many of whom lack access to the surgery that could transform their lives. Smile Train and similar organizations saw increased visibility and support following the film's success, helping fund surgeries for countless other children who might otherwise have faced the same isolation Pinki once knew.

Her story also challenged stigmas surrounding physical differences and disabilities in India and beyond, sparking conversations about the intersection of poverty, healthcare access, and social inclusion.

## Conclusion

Pinki Sonkar's journey—from a shy, ostracized child hiding her face in a rural Indian village to a celebrated figure at the Academy Awards—stands as a testament to the life-changing power of accessible medical care and the universal human desire to be seen, accepted, and loved. Her story, immortalized in "Smile Pinki," continues to inspire advocacy for children with cleft conditions worldwide, proving that sometimes the smallest surgical interventions can lead to the most profound transformations—not just of a smile, but of an entire life's trajectory.
